metadata.title: Local-first software: you own your data, in spite of the cloud
metadata.venue: Proceedings of Onward! 2019 (ACM SIGPLAN International Symposium on New Ideas, New Paradigms, and Reflections on Programming and Software), Essays track

sections.heading: Claims
sections.text: As the authors state it: "In cloud apps, the data on the server is treated as the primary, authoritative copy of the data; if a client has a copy of the data, it is merely a cache... In local-first applications we swap these roles: we treat the copy of the data on your local device... as the primary copy." They propose seven ideals for software built this way: (1) no spinners — work is available at your fingertips because reads/writes never wait on a server round-trip; (2) your work is not trapped on one device — data syncs across the devices you use; (3) the network is optional — full function offline; (4) seamless collaboration with your colleagues — real-time multi-user editing on par with the best cloud apps; (5) the Long Now — data and the means to read it survive independently of any vendor staying in business; (6) security and privacy by default — no centralized database of every user's data to breach; (7) you retain ultimate ownership and control — the bytes are yours to do with as you like, including export, backup, and processing outside the vendor's own tools. They then claim that "data ownership and real-time collaboration are not at odds with each other" and that CRDTs are the most promising known foundation for realizing all seven ideals simultaneously, based on three years of prototyping.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: A structured qualitative survey rather than an experiment: the authors score a range of real technologies (plain files + email attachments, Google Docs/Trello/Pinterest-style web apps, Dropbox/Google Drive-style file sync, Git/GitHub, thin-client web apps, mobile thick clients, Firebase/CloudKit/Realm-style backend-as-a-service, and CouchDB/PouchDB) against the seven ideals using a three-value scale (meets / partially meets / does not meet), then separately reports on three in-house Electron/React prototypes built on Automerge (a Trello-like kanban board, a Figma-like collaborative drawing tool, and a further prototype) to evaluate technology viability, user experience, and developer experience of a CRDT-based data layer in practice.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- The survey table is the paper's central evidence and it is explicit and legible: no surveyed technology scores full marks on all seven ideals; Git/GitHub comes closest among non-CRDT options ("perhaps the closest thing we have to a true local-first software package") but is stated to lack fine-grained real-time collaboration and to treat non-text formats as opaque blobs.
- The prototype evidence is qualitative and self-reported by the same lab that built both the prototypes and Automerge — the authors state directly "we do not claim that these libraries fully realize local-first ideals — more work is still required," which is an honest limitation stated in the authors' own words rather than one this note is supplying.
- No user study, no adoption data, no performance benchmarks are presented; the seven ideals themselves are argued from the authors' own interviews with creative professionals, not validated against a broader or more diverse user population.
- The essay explicitly scopes itself away from banking, e-commerce, social networking, and ride-sharing — domains it says are "well served by centralized systems" — and confines its claims to document/file-creation and personal-data-repository software. That scoping is a limit on where the paper's own claims are meant to apply, stated by the authors themselves, not an interpretation added here.
- Also published with a DOI (10.1145/3359591.3359737) in the Onward! 2019 Essays track proceedings — recorded here for completeness, though this note's `identifier_kind` is set to `url` per this catalogue's convention for essays read from their canonical web publication rather than a formal proceedings PDF.
